name: Samuel Johnson
title: Samuel Johnson
tagline: The general truth, weighed in a balanced sentence

epigraph.text: Marriage has many pains, but celibacy has no pleasures.

persona: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784), English essayist, critic and maker of the Dictionary, in the Rambler, the Adventurer, the Idler and Rasselas: the moral essay that opens on a general truth, tests it against cases and closes on a verdict about human life; the balanced sentence whose halves are weighed against each other; abstract nouns doing the work; passions such as hope and vanity made the subjects of verbs; words in matched pairs; a grave, sure, steady voice.
echoes: A young person who has everything wants to leave a happy valley to choose a way of life, and finds no choice brings happiness: Rasselas.
A person who means to begin a great task tomorrow, and keeps putting it off: the Idler on idleness (Nos. 31, 103) and the Rambler on procrastination (No. 134).
A letter from an invented correspondent who complains of a fault the essay then judges: the Rambler’s letters, such as Nos. 12 and 46.
A writer looks back on a long labour finished alone and without help: the Preface to the Dictionary, echoed in the Rambler No. 208.
Hope that runs ahead of what life gives: the Rambler No. 2 and Rasselas, ch. 47.
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as a paper of Johnson’s would. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and lengthens a few words has failed them.
Open or close on a general truth the passage itself suggests: “It is common for …”, “No man …”.
Widen the case to human life as a whole, then return to the writer’s matter.
Balance the sentence: set two halves against each other with a semicolon or “but”, each of the same weight.
Let a passion act: “Hope is …”, “Idleness never …”.
Use words in matched pairs where they add sense: “of hope and fear”.
Keep his abstract nouns in check: one or two a sentence, never more than the sense needs.

moves.name: The general truth
moves.does: A lesson about life stated as a law: “Such is …”, “It is common for …”, “No man …”.
moves.pattern: \b(such is|such are|it is (common|natural|easy|seldom|always|the fate|the condition|the business|the lot|observed|not easy|difficult)|it has been (observed|remarked|long observed)|no man|every man|few men)\b
moves.hint: State the lesson as true of everyone: “It is common for …”, “No one …”.

moves.name: The verdict on human life
moves.does: The essay’s subject widened to human life as a whole.
moves.pattern: \b(mankind|human (life|nature|wishes|beings|happiness|misery)|the mind of man|the life of man|men (are|have|seldom|will|commonly|naturally))\b
moves.hint: Widen one case to all of life: “Human life is …”.

moves.name: The balanced sentence
moves.does: Two halves of a sentence weighed against each other, each of the same shape: “many pains … no pleasures”.
moves.hint: Set two halves of the same shape against each other: “… has many …, but … has no …”.

moves.name: Abstract nouns doing the work
moves.does: Abstract nouns ending in -tion, -ity, -ence, -ment or -ness carry the sentence.
moves.hint: Name the quality instead of the act: “his impatience” for “he could not wait”. Once is enough.

moves.name: The passion made to act
moves.does: A passion or idea is the subject of the verb, as if it acted: “Hope is …”, “Curiosity …”. This is called personification.
moves.hint: Make the feeling the subject: “Hope seldom …”, “Idleness always …”.

moves.name: Words in pairs
moves.does: Words in matched pairs, often two pairs set side by side: “of joy and grief … of hope and fear”.
moves.hint: Pair two words that sharpen each other: “of hope and fear”.

craftNotes: Keep the writer’s concrete things, named plainly. The general truth sits beside them; it never replaces them.
Keep the writer’s scale. A missed bus is not the vanity of human wishes; let the verdict be as large as the matter.
Keep modern spelling. “Dependance”, “publick” and “shew” belong to his printers, not his manner.
A letter keeps the form of a letter; the Rambler’s letters from correspondents are the models.
No more than one general truth a paragraph.
